RagShortTexts: Berke Khan waged war against Hulagu over Baghdad's destruction, allying with Mamluk Egypt.

Variants.Content: Hulagu Khan's sack of Baghdad and the execution of Caliph al-Musta'sim in 1258 provoked the anger of Berke Khan, the Muslim ruler of the Golden Horde. Berke declared a vendetta for the caliph and allied with the Mamluk sultanate of Egypt against the Ilkhanate. His cavalry struck deep into the Caucasus, and the campaigns along the Terek River ended in winter carnage as the frozen water broke under men and horses. The war split the Mongol world into rival khanates with opposing interests. The Ilkhanate's grip on Persia and Mesopotamia now faced a hostile northern neighbour and a southern enemy in Cairo.

Genghis Khan's Yassa forbade fratricide among the golden princes, yet religious zeal and rich pastures in Shirvan broke the ancestral bans. Berke tried to keep the Aegean maritime corridors open to Cairo, which was the main Mamluk link to trade and to allies in the west. Each court sent sealed letters to test the others' resolve.

On the frozen Terek, steppe tumens faced other tumens armed in exactly the same way. Their arrows whined off lamellar armour of identical pattern, and the men knew each other's horse-tack. It was the grimmest winter many of them had ever seen, with cracked ice swallowing thousands. Keep your bow dry and your boots on, because the next crossing will be worse.
